title: Finkelstein reaction
subtitle: Iodide swaps for chloride in acetone

reactants.caption: iodide + chloroethane
reactants.learnerPrompt: Iodide replaces chlorine. Draw the arrows.
hintTiers: Iodide is the nucleophile and chloride the leaving group. Which carbon carries the chlorine?
Iodide attacks the CH₂ carbon from the back as the C–Cl bond breaks. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair on iodide forms a bond to the CH₂ carbon. Arrow 2: the C–Cl bond breaks, and its pair goes onto chlorine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chlorine is the leaving group and carries δ− charge. Iodide attacks the δ+ carbon.
The CH₃ carbon has no leaving group. Attack the carbon bonded to chlorine.
The C–Cl pair goes to chlorine, the more electronegative atom.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Octet check: carbon would now have 10 electrons. What has to leave as the nucleophile arrives?
A primary carbocation will not form. In SN2, iodide pushes in as chloride leaves.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Iodide and chloride are both good leaving groups, so this step could run backwards. Sodium chloride precipitates from acetone, which removes chloride and drives the reaction forward (Le Chatelier).

mechanismSummary: Finkelstein reaction: an SN2 halide exchange. Iodide is a large, polarisable and excellent nucleophile. The reaction is reversible, but sodium chloride is insoluble in acetone and precipitates, while sodium iodide stays dissolved, so the equilibrium is pulled towards iodoethane.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 15
